# Time-to-event data and censoring {#sec-survival-data}

```{r}
#| label: setup-ch1
#| include: false
library(survival)
library(dplyr)
```

{{< include ./_extensions/r-wasm/live/_knitr.qmd >}}

::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## In this chapter
**The question.** Patients with advanced lung cancer are followed up after joining a study. Some die during follow-up, but many are still alive when the study ends. How can we describe how long these patients survive?

**By the end of this chapter you will be able to:**

- recognise time-to-event data and its three ingredients: a time origin, an event and a time scale;
- explain what **censoring** is, and why ignoring it gives the wrong answer;
- state the assumption of **non-informative censoring**;
- create a survival outcome in R with `Surv()`.
:::

This chapter has your first **live R exercises**: code boxes you can edit
and run in the page itself. @sec-live-exercises explains how they work.

## What makes survival data special?

In **survival analysis** (also called *time-to-event analysis*), the outcome
is the *time until an event happens*. The event might be death, relapse,
hospital discharge, injury, or a machine failing. Every observation needs
three things:

1. A clear **time origin**. When does the clock start? Diagnosis,
   randomisation, the start of treatment?
2. A clear **event** definition.
3. A **time scale**. Days, months or years since the origin, or age.

What makes this kind of data special is **censoring**. For some people the
study ends, or they drop out, *before* we see their event. All we know is
that their event time is *longer than* the time we observed. The word
comes from *censorship*: like a censor blacking out the rest of a
document, the rest of the patient's story is hidden from us.

::: {.callout-important}
## Censoring is not missing data
A censored observation still tells us something useful. Suppose a patient
was last seen alive and event-free after 2.3 years of follow-up. We don't
know when they will die, but we do know they survived at least 2.3 years. Throwing that information away, or
treating 2.3 years as if it were the event time, biases the results.
Survival methods use exactly what we know, and nothing more.
:::

### Types of censoring

All the censoring in this book is **right censoring**: we know the event
happened *after* a certain time (to the right of it, on a timeline). It
has three common causes:

- **Administrative censoring.** The study ends. Patients who joined late
  are followed for less time.
- **Loss to follow-up.** The patient moves away or withdraws.
- **Competing events.** The patient dies of something else before the
  event of interest. Strictly, this isn't censoring at all: someone who has
  died can never relapse. Treating these deaths as censored is a common
  mistake (@sec-competing).

Kaplan–Meier and Cox methods assume that censoring is **non-informative**.
At any time, people who are censored must have the same future risk as
people who stay under observation. If the sickest patients drop out because
they're sick, this assumption is broken. Chapter 4 has an app that shows
what happens then (@sec-informative).

## Why not just use the average time, or logistic regression?

- The **mean observed time** is biased downwards, because censored times
  are shorter than the true event times.
- Using the **mean among people who had the event** throws away the
  censored people. It is biased towards fast events.
- **Logistic regression** on "died: yes/no" ignores *when* the event
  happened. It also mixes up people followed for 1 month with people
  followed for 5 years.

The app below makes this concrete.

## Interactive app: what censoring does {#sec-app-censoring}

Each line is a patient. Patients join the study at different times during
the *recruitment period*, and the study stops at a fixed calendar date. A
filled dot ● is an observed event. A cross ✕ is a censored observation.
Tick *Show what we never see* to reveal the true event times hidden by
censoring.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
import {makeRandom, mean, quiz} from "./js/survtools.js"
```

::: {.app}
```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof c1Scen = Inputs.radio(["Default", "Short study (2 years)", "No drop-out, 10-year study"], {value: "Default", label: "Scenario"})
c1P = ({"Default": {}, "Short study (2 years)": {"study": 2}, "No drop-out, 10-year study": {"drop": 0, "study": 10}})[c1Scen]
viewof c1 = Inputs.form({
  n:       Inputs.range([5, 40],  {value: c1P.n ?? 20,  step: 1,   label: "Patients shown"}),
  accrual: Inputs.range([0, 4],   {value: c1P.accrual ?? 2,   step: 0.5, label: "Recruitment period (yrs)"}),
  study:   Inputs.range([1, 10],  {value: c1P.study ?? 5,   step: 0.5, label: "Study length (yrs)"}),
  median:  Inputs.range([0.5, 8], {value: c1P.median ?? 3,   step: 0.5, label: "True median survival (yrs)"}),
  drop:    Inputs.range([0, 0.5], {value: c1P.drop ?? 0.1, step: 0.05, label: "Drop-out rate (per yr)"}),
  seed:    Inputs.range([1, 100], {value: c1P.seed ?? 7,   step: 1,   label: "Random seed"})
}, {template: formGrid})
formGrid = inputs => html`<div class="form-grid">${Object.values(inputs)}</div>`
viewof c1view = Inputs.radio(["Calendar time", "Time since entry"], {value: "Calendar time", label: "Time axis"})
viewof c1truth = Inputs.toggle({label: "Show what we never see", value: false})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
function simCensoring(p, n, seed) {
  const r = makeRandom(seed);
  const rate = Math.LN2 / p.median;
  const studyEnd = Math.max(p.study, p.accrual);
  return Array.from({length: n}, (_, i) => {
    const entry = r.unif() * p.accrual;
    const tEvent = r.exp(rate);
    const tDrop = p.drop > 0 ? r.exp(p.drop) : Infinity;
    const tAdmin = studyEnd - entry;
    const time = Math.min(tEvent, tDrop, tAdmin);
    const status = tEvent <= Math.min(tDrop, tAdmin) ? 1 : 0;
    const reason = status ? "Event" : (tDrop < tAdmin ? "Censored: dropped out" : "Censored: study ended");
    return {id: i + 1, entry, tEvent, time, status, reason};
  });
}
c1data = simCensoring(c1, c1.n, c1.seed)
c1big  = simCensoring(c1, 5000, c1.seed + 1000)
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const cal = c1view === "Calendar time";
  const studyEnd = Math.max(c1.study, c1.accrual);
  const d = c1data.map(p => ({...p,
    x0: cal ? p.entry : 0,
    x1: cal ? p.entry + p.time : p.time,
    xt: cal ? p.entry + p.tEvent : p.tEvent}));
  const hidden = d.filter(p => !p.status);
  return Plot.plot({
    height: 120 + 14 * c1.n, marginLeft: 50,
    x: {label: cal ? "Calendar time since study opened (years) →" : "Time since patient entered (years) →",
        domain: [0, Math.max(studyEnd, ...(c1truth ? d.map(p => Math.min(p.xt, studyEnd * 2)) : [studyEnd]))]},
    y: {label: "Patient", tickFormat: d => d, domain: d.map(p => p.id)},
    color: {legend: true, domain: ["Event", "Censored: study ended", "Censored: dropped out"],
            range: ["#D55E00", "#0072B2", "#CC79A7"]},
    marks: [
      cal ? Plot.ruleX([studyEnd], {stroke: "#888", strokeDasharray: "4,3"}) : null,
      cal && c1.accrual > 0 ? Plot.rectX([{x1: 0, x2: c1.accrual}], {x1: "x1", x2: "x2", fill: "#999", fillOpacity: 0.08}) : null,
      c1truth ? Plot.ruleY(hidden, {y: "id", x1: "x1", x2: p => Math.min(p.xt, studyEnd * 2), stroke: "#aaa", strokeDasharray: "2,3"}) : null,
      c1truth ? Plot.dot(hidden, {y: "id", x: p => Math.min(p.xt, studyEnd * 2), stroke: "#aaa", r: 3.5}) : null,
      Plot.ruleY(d, {y: "id", x1: "x0", x2: "x1", stroke: "reason", strokeWidth: 2.5}),
      Plot.dot(d.filter(p => p.status), {y: "id", x: "x1", fill: "reason", r: 4.5}),
      Plot.dot(d.filter(p => !p.status), {y: "id", x: "x1", stroke: "reason", symbol: "times", r: 5, strokeWidth: 2})
    ]
  });
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const big = c1big;
  const trueMean = c1.median / Math.LN2;
  const rows = [
    {Quantity: "True mean survival time", Value: trueMean, Comment: "What we want to know"},
    {Quantity: "Mean of observed times (ignoring censoring)", Value: mean(big.map(d => d.time)), Comment: "Too low: censored times are cut short"},
    {Quantity: "Mean time among those with an event", Value: mean(big.filter(d => d.status).map(d => d.time)) || NaN, Comment: "Too low: long survivors are left out"},

  ];

}
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Things to try
For each one, **predict first**: decide what you expect to see, then pick the scenario and check. Committing to a prediction, even a wrong one, makes the result stick.

1. **Predict:** if every patient's line started at 0, which patients would
   have the shortest lines? *Then* switch the time axis to **Time since
   entry**. This is how survival software sees the data.
2. **Predict:** if the study lasts only 2 years, will the two naive averages
   move closer to the truth or further away? *Then* pick **Short study
   (2 years)**.
3. **Predict:** what happens to the naive averages when almost no one is
   censored? *Then* pick **No drop-out, 10-year study**.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Answers: what you should see
1. **Time since entry.** Every line now starts at 0. Patients who joined
   near the end of the recruitment period have the shortest lines ending in
   a blue ✕. They were censored early because the study closed, not because
   of anything about their health. That's why administrative censoring is
   usually *non-informative*.
2. **Study length 2 years.** Most lines now end in a ✕. With the other
   settings at their defaults, about 80% of patients are censored. The naive
   mean falls to about 0.8 years (truth: 4.3), and the mean among those with
   an event to about 0.6 years. Both get worse the shorter the follow-up.
   The Kaplan–Meier method (Chapter 2) uses the censored patients properly.
3. **No drop-out, 10-year study.** Only people still alive after 8–10 years
   are censored, about 13% of patients. The naive mean rises to about
   3.8 years, much closer to 4.3. It's still too low, because the few
   censored patients are the longest survivors. Censoring causes the bias:
   the less of it there is, the smaller the bias.
:::

## Survival data in R: the `Surv()` object

We'll use the `lung` dataset from the **survival** package. It has
survival times (in days) for 228 patients with advanced lung cancer.

```{r}
#| label: lung-head
head(survival::lung)
```

The important columns are `time` (days of follow-up) and `status`. Note
that in this dataset `status` is coded **1 = censored, 2 = dead**. R
accepts 1/2, but 0/1 or `FALSE/TRUE` are clearer, so we recode. We also
turn `sex` into a labelled factor.

```{r}
#| label: lung-clean
lung <- survival::lung |>
  mutate(
    status = status - 1,                              # 0 = censored, 1 = died
    sex    = factor(sex, levels = 1:2, labels = c("Male", "Female")),
    time_m = time / 30.44                             # follow-up in months
  )

table(lung$status)        # 63 censored, 165 deaths
```

`Surv(time, status)` combines the two columns into one survival
outcome. Censored times are printed with a `+`:

```{r}
#| label: surv-object
Surv(lung$time, lung$status)[1:15]
```

Almost every survival function in R takes a formula with `Surv()` on the
left-hand side, for example:

```r
survfit(Surv(time, status) ~ sex, data = lung)         # Kaplan-Meier, Ch 2
coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ sex + age, data = lung)     # Cox model, Ch 3
```

:::: {.optional}
::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Going further (optional): other forms of `Surv()`
- `Surv(start, stop, event)`: *counting-process* form. Use it for
  time-varying covariates and delayed entry (left truncation).
- `Surv(time, event, type = "interval")`: interval-censored data, where you
  only know the event happened between two visits.
:::
::::

## Live R exercises
The exercises in this book run **real R inside the web page**. There's
nothing to install.

- The first time you open a page with exercises, R loads in the background.
  This takes 10–30 seconds, and it's quicker on later visits. Some exercises
  also download extra packages the first time you run them, so that first
  run is slower.

::: {.hint exercise="ex_surv"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint 1
`status` is the column being recoded. `Surv()` takes the time column first, then the status column.
:::
:::

::: {.hint exercise="ex_surv"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint 2
Every blank is either `time` or `status`.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_surv"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution
```r
lung <- survival::lung
lung$status <- lung$status - 1
Surv(lung$time, lung$status)[1:10]
table(lung$status)
```

The censored patients are the ones marked `+`: among the first 10, the 3rd
(1010+ days) and the 6th (1022+ days). 165 patients died and 63 were
censored.
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_surv
#| check: true
env <- .envir_result
if (is.null(env$lung) || !identical(env$lung$status, survival::lung$status - 1)) {
  list(correct = FALSE,
       message = "The recoding isn't right yet: the first blank should make <code>status</code> 0 for censored and 1 for died (<code>lung$status - 1</code>).")
} else if (!grepl("Surv\\(\\s*lung\\$time\\s*,\\s*lung\\$status", .user_code)) {
  list(correct = FALSE,
       message = "<code>Surv()</code> takes the follow-up time first, then the status: <code>Surv(lung$time, lung$status)</code>.")
} else if (!is.table(.result) || !identical(as.vector(.result), c(63L, 165L))) {
  list(correct = FALSE,
       message = "The last line should count the recoded status values: <code>table(lung$status)</code>.")
} else {
  list(correct = TRUE,
       message = "Correct! 165 patients died and 63 were censored. Which of the first 10 were censored? (Look for the +.)")
}
```

## Quick quiz {.unnumbered}

Choose an answer to each question. You'll get instant feedback and can change your answer as often as you like.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
quiz([
 {
  "q": "A patient joined the study 2 years before it closed and was alive on the closing date. How should their record be entered?",
  "options": [
   "Event at 2 years",
   "Censored at 2 years",
   "Excluded, because their outcome is missing",
   "Censored at the total length of the study"
  ],
  "answer": 1,
  "why": "We know they were event-free for 2 years, and nothing after that. So time = 2, status = 0.",
  "hints": [
   "They didn't have the event, so status must be 0 (censored).",
   "",
   "Excluding them throws away 2 years of event-free follow-up and biases survival downwards.",
   "Time is measured from *their* entry, not from when the study opened."
  ]
 },
 {
  "q": "Which of these most clearly breaks the 'non-informative censoring' assumption?",
  "options": [
   "Patients recruited late are followed for less time",
   "A patient moves abroad for a new job",
   "Patients withdraw because they become too unwell to attend visits",
   "The study closes on a fixed date"
  ],
  "answer": 2,
  "why": "Those patients are censored *because* their risk is high. People left in the risk set are healthier than the people who leave it, so survival is overestimated.",
  "hints": [
   "Late recruitment is unrelated to prognosis, so this is fine.",
   "Moving for a job is (probably) unrelated to the risk of the event.",
   "",
   "A fixed closing date is unrelated to any one patient's risk."
  ]
 },
 {
  "q": "Why is the average of observed follow-up times a poor estimate of average survival?",
  "options": [
   "It's too high, because long survivors dominate",
   "It's too low, because censored times are shorter than the true event times",
   "It's fine as long as the sample is large",
   "It's only a problem when two events happen at the same time"
  ],
  "answer": 1,
  "why": "Each censored time is a lower bound on the true event time, so averaging them pulls the estimate down. A bigger sample doesn't fix this.",
  "hints": [
   "Look at the app again: the naive means were always *below* the truth.",
   "",
   "A bias doesn't shrink with sample size. More data just gives a more precise wrong answer.",
   "Ties are a minor technical issue. Censoring is the real problem."
  ]
 },
 {
  "q": "In <code>survival::lung</code>, <code>status</code> is coded 1/2. After <code>status - 1</code>, what does <code>status = 1</code> mean?",
  "options": [
   "Censored",
   "Died",
   "Lost to follow-up",
   "Alive at 1 year"
  ],
  "answer": 1,
  "why": "The original coding is 1 = censored, 2 = dead. Subtracting 1 gives the usual 0 = censored, 1 = event.",
  "hints": [
   "Censored becomes 0.",
   "",
   "Lost to follow-up is a kind of censoring, which is coded 0.",
   "status records what happened at the end of follow-up, not at a fixed time."
  ]
 }
])
```

## Exercise

### Exercise 1.1

*These are live exercises: edit the code, click **Run Code**, and your answer is checked automatically. See @sec-live-exercises if you haven't used them before.*

1. How many patients in `lung` have a missing value in `ph.ecog`
   (performance score)?
2. What is the longest follow-up time? Was that patient censored, or did
   they die? Make this the last line, so it can be checked.
3. Write down, in one sentence, what the "time origin" and "event" are for
   `lung`. (Hint: the help page, `?lung`, describes the variables.)

```{webr}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_lung_explore
library(survival)
lung <- survival::lung
lung$status <- lung$status - 1        # 0 = censored, 1 = died
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_lung_explore
#| caption: "Exercise 1.1: exploring the lung data"
# 1. Number of missing values in ph.ecog


# 2. The row with the longest follow-up time: show its time and status (last line)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_lung_explore"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint 1
`is.na()` gives `TRUE` for each missing value, and `sum()` counts the `TRUE`s.
:::
:::

::: {.hint exercise="ex_lung_explore"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint 2
`which.max(lung$time)` gives the row number of the longest time, so `lung[which.max(lung$time), c("time", "status")]` shows that row.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_lung_explore"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution
```r
sum(is.na(lung$ph.ecog))
lung[which.max(lung$time), c("time", "status")]
```

One patient has a missing `ph.ecog`. The longest follow-up is 1022 days, and
that patient was **censored** (`status = 0`): they were still alive at their
last follow-up. For part 3, `?lung` says time is "survival time in days",
measured from enrolment, and the event is death from any cause.
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_lung_explore
#| check: true
if (!grepl("is\\.na\\s*\\(\\s*lung\\$ph\\.ecog", .user_code)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "warning",
       message = "For part 1, count the missing values with <code>sum(is.na(lung$ph.ecog))</code>.")
} else if (is.data.frame(.result) && all(c("time", "status") %in% names(.result)) &&
           nrow(.result) == 1 && .result$time == 1022) {
  list(correct = TRUE,
       message = "Correct! The longest follow-up is 1022 days, and <code>status = 0</code>, so that patient was censored, not dead. (And one patient has a missing <code>ph.ecog</code>.)")
} else if (is.numeric(.result) && length(.result) == 1 && .result == 1022) {
  list(correct = FALSE,
       message = "Yes, the longest time is 1022 days. Now show that patient's <code>status</code> too: <code>lung[which.max(lung$time), c('time', 'status')]</code>.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE,
       message = "Make the last line show the time and status of the patient with the longest follow-up. Try <code>which.max(lung$time)</code>.")
}
```

## Summary

::: {.callout-important icon="false"}
## Key points
- Survival data record the **time until an event**. You need a clear time origin, a clear event and a time scale.
- A **censored** observation tells us only that the event happened *after* the last follow-up. It isn't missing data. It carries real information.
- Ignoring censoring gives the wrong answer: averages of observed times are too low, and yes/no analyses ignore *when* events happen.
- Survival methods assume censoring is **non-informative**: people who are censored have the same future risk as those still being followed.
- In R, `Surv(time, status)` combines follow-up time and event status (1 = event, 0 = censored). In `lung`, `status` must be recoded from 1/2 to 0/1 first.
:::

**Answering the question.** We can't just average the follow-up times, because 63 of the 228 patients were censored, so their follow-up times are shorter than their true survival times. We need a method that uses the information in censored patients correctly. That's the Kaplan–Meier estimator, in the next chapter.

## Further reading

All of these are free to read online unless marked otherwise. The whole
book's reading list, grouped by topic, is in @sec-further-reading.

- @clark2003: **Start here.** A clear, non-technical introduction to survival data, censoring and Kaplan–Meier curves, written for clinicians and researchers.
- @ucla_survival: Free workshop materials with R code, covering how to set up survival data in R and run first analyses. A useful second explanation alongside this book.
- @leung1997: *More advanced.* The different kinds of censoring, and why the non-informative censoring assumption matters. (May need institutional access.)
